opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think "more powerful" is a phrase people use a bit loosely, so the first thing I try to do is pin down what we actually mean by it.

One way I've come to think about optimizers, and this is a big part of the perspective in our nested learning work, is that an optimizer is itself a kind of associative memory. When you run gradient descent with momentum, the momentum term is basically a memory that compresses the history of past gradients. It's learning a mapping, in a sense, from what it has seen to what update it should produce. Once you look at it that way, you can ask the same questions about an optimizer that you'd ask about any memory module: what's its capacity, what objective is it implicitly optimizing internally, how does it decide what to keep and what to forget, and how expressive is the function it uses to map inputs to outputs?

From that angle, a claim that optimizer A is more powerful than optimizer B can mean a few concrete things. It might mean the memory is more expressive. Plain momentum is essentially a linear, very low-capacity memory: an exponential moving average. If you replace that with something that has a richer internal objective, or a deeper, nonlinear memory, it can in principle capture more structure in the gradient history. Or it might mean it has a better internal objective. A lot of popular optimizers implicitly minimize a fairly simple, dot-product-style similarity, and you can argue that's not the right objective for compressing gradients. Something closer to a regression-style loss can make better use of the same capacity. Or it might mean better adaptivity: how well it handles non-stationarity, whether it can adjust what it remembers as the loss landscape changes during training.

So I'd say there's a meaningful, almost theoretical sense in which one optimizer can be strictly more expressive than another, in that it can represent the update rules of the other as special cases plus more. That's a real claim and you can sometimes show it formally.

But I'm careful about jumping from "more expressive" to "better in practice." More expressive memory costs compute and memory, it can be harder to tune, and it can be less stable. And the empirical results depend a lot on scale, architecture, data, and how carefully the baselines were tuned. A lot of "new optimizer beats Adam" results shrink once someone tunes Adam properly or runs at larger scale. So when I see such a claim, I want to know: more powerful in what sense, at what cost, and does it hold up under fair comparison and across scales?

The part I find most exciting is that this framing blurs the line between architecture and optimizer. If the optimizer is a memory and the layers are memories, then designing a better optimizer and designing a better architecture start to look like the same problem, just at different levels and different update frequencies. That opens up a design space that I think we've barely explored, rather than treating the optimizer as a fixed tool we bolt on at the end.

r001.rationale: The response says empirical results depend on scale, architecture, data, and baseline tuning, and asks whether a claim holds across scales—making clear that comparative performance depends on the problem setup.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So, I think the honest answer is that "more powerful" is almost never a well-defined claim on its own. When people say optimizer A is more powerful than optimizer B, what they usually mean is that on some benchmark, with some architecture, under some compute budget, A got a lower loss or converged faster. And that's a real result, but it's a result about a very specific setting, not about the optimizer in the abstract.

The way I like to think about it is that an optimizer is really a prior. It encodes assumptions about the geometry of the loss landscape, about how gradients relate to each other across steps, about how much memory of past updates is useful. Adam, for instance, assumes that per-coordinate scaling matters a lot. Second-order methods assume curvature information is worth the cost of estimating it. So when one optimizer beats another, what you're really learning is that its assumptions matched that landscape better. Change the model, change the data distribution, change the scale, and the ranking can flip.

That's part of why I'm drawn to framing optimization and memory together. If you think of an optimizer as something that compresses the history of gradients into a state and then uses that state to decide the next step, then "more powerful" starts to have a more concrete meaning: how expressive is that state, how much of the past can it actually retain and use, and at what cost? That gives you a dimension to compare along, rather than just a leaderboard.

The other thing I'd push on is that a lot of these comparisons aren't apples to apples. Hyperparameters for the baseline are often inherited from years of community tuning, while the new method gets tuned carefully by the people proposing it. Or the opposite happens. So I tend to trust claims more when they come with scaling curves rather than single points, when the comparison is at matched wall-clock or matched memory and not just matched steps, and when the result holds across more than one architecture family. If a method only wins in one narrow regime, that's still interesting, but it's a statement about the regime, not about power.

So I'd say: be skeptical of the word "powerful," ask what assumption the optimizer is making, and ask under what conditions that assumption is actually true. That reframing usually tells you more than the benchmark number does.

r001.rationale: The response says optimizer rankings can change with the model, data distribution, scale, and benchmark conditions, so which performs better depends on the problem setup.

astra-6.text:
I think the first question is: what do we mean by more powerful? Do we mean it converges faster, it reaches a better solution, or it works well across a broader set of problems? Those are different claims.

An optimizer makes assumptions about the problem through the information it keeps and how it uses that information to update the parameters. Momentum keeps a history of gradients, for example. That history can be useful, but whether it helps depends on the structure of the problem.

So I’m cautious about saying one optimizer is universally more powerful than another. I would rather ask: under what assumptions, with what computational budget, and for which objective? If we make those explicit, then we can have a meaningful comparison.

r001.rationale: The response says whether momentum helps depends on the problem’s structure and frames optimizer comparisons around assumptions, budget, and objective.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first question is, what do we mean by more powerful? Do we mean that it converges faster, that it reaches a better solution, or that it can use information that another optimizer cannot? Those are different claims.

An optimizer is itself a learning algorithm. It has some state, it receives gradients, and it updates that state and the parameters. So you can look at the optimizer in terms of what information it remembers and how it uses that information. Momentum, for example, gives you a memory of past gradients. More sophisticated update rules can maintain different kinds of statistics.

But having a richer update rule doesn’t automatically mean you’ll get better results on every problem. You have to specify the objective, the assumptions, and the computational budget. Otherwise, saying one optimizer is more powerful than another is a little too broad.

r001.rationale: It says a richer update rule does not guarantee better results on every problem and that comparisons require specifying the objective, assumptions, and computational budget.
